newsitem.title: GERMANY: POLL - German economic growth to miss 1997 govt goal.
newsitem.headline: POLL - German economic growth to miss 1997 govt goal.

text.p: German economic growth will pick up pace as the year goes on, but will undershoot the government's forecast of 2.5 percent expansion in 1997, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

While the average of economists' forecasts put quarter-on-quarter GDP growth at 2.4 percent in the final quarter of 1997, sluggish performance in the second and third quarters, when respective rates of 2.0 and 1.9 percent are forecast, will dull the annual figures.
Not until 1998 will the economy begin to grow at a pace above 2.5 percent, and analysts on average expect economic growth for the whole of next year to reach 2.7 percent.

Of around 30 analysts surveyed, Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt, was forecasting the highest growth rates for 1998, predicting 3.3 percent, driven partly by the weak deutschemark exchange rate.
"Even that is at the lower end of what we might expect," said Schmieding. "The currency is extremely supportive of growth and should add more than 1.0 percent to growth levels in 1998."

Schmieding said the mark had lost almost eight percent on a trade-weighted basis on a year-on-year view. "Also we will have the end of fiscal tightening in Germany in 1998, which this year probably subtracted half a percentage point from growth," Schmieding said.
"Next year that loss won't be there any more."
At the other end of the scale, economists at Helaba in Frankfurt expected growth of only 2.1 percent in 1998, up from a meagre 1.9 percent this year.
Either way, inflation, it appears, will remain subdued well into 1998, with consumer price (CPI) inflation nudging up to just 2.1 percent by the fourth quarter of next year, mean forecasts showed.

The average annual CPI growth rate was forecast at 1.6 percent for 1997 and 1.9 percent in 1998, with most analysts saying price pressure was unlikely to become a problem, despite the weakness of the mark.
Producer prices are also expected to remain subdued, average forecasts putting their rise at 1.1 percent in 1997 and 1.7 percent in 1998, the poll showed.
Unemployment, however, will remain a sharp thorn in Germany's side for many months to come.
Average forecasts for the jobless rate, already 11.1 percent, were of an annual rate of 11.3 percent in 1997, falling only slightly to 11.0 percent in 1998.

The most pessimistic forecast on jobs came from the DIW economic research institute in Berlin -- one of Germany's six leading institutes -- which expects unemployment to rise to 11.4 percent this year and continue its upward path in 1998, reaching 12.1 percent.

Bank Julius Baer and Industrie Kreditbank (IKB) gave the lowest forecasts for 1997, expecting 11.0 percent joblessness, but while Julius Baer saw that rate falling in 1998 to 10.7 percent, IKB said it expected 11.0 percent unemployment to persist through 1998.
